facts.claim: Chiang et al. (2024) describe Chatbot Arena, since renamed Arena: people put one question to two unnamed models and vote for the better reply, and the votes become a ranking. It had over 240,000 votes when the paper came out.
Singh et al. (2025) found some providers test many private versions on Chatbot Arena and publish only the best; Meta tested 27 before Llama 4’s release.
Zhang et al. (2024) wrote GSM1k, fresh maths questions like a popular public test, and some models scored up to 8 points lower on it: they had partly learned the public test itself.
Anthropic’s price list (checked 2026-10-30) charges per million tokens with output at five times input, from $0.10 in and $0.50 out for Claude Haiku 5.5 up to $10 in and $50 out for Claude Fable 5.1.

NVIDIA’s benchmarking guide (checked 2026-10-30) defines time to first token as the wait from sending a request to the first token back, and the end-to-end wait as the time until the whole reply has arrived.

Chen, Zaharia and Zou (2023) found model prices differing up to 100 times, and that trying cheaper models first, moving up only when an answer looked unsure, matched GPT-4 in their tests for up to 98% less.
Liang et al. (2022, HELM) scored 30 models on 7 measures, from accuracy to efficiency and fairness, across 16 core uses, so that trade-offs between them show rather than one ranking.
Anthropic’s deprecations page (checked 2026-10-30) promises at least 60 days’ notice before retiring a public model, and advises testing the replacement well before that date.
OpenAI’s prompt engineering guide (checked 2026-10-30) advises pinning live apps to a model snapshot, one fixed dated version, and building tests that measure behaviour as you change model versions.
